statements.justification: Values match: MTTP -6.46 (RNA) and -8.50 (protein) in the DBD mutant, SUMO mutant near zero; HNF1A -0.39 not relevant. Both cited abstracts support HNF4α control of MTTP/apoB and MTP's role in apoB assembly. The paper reports cholesterol/lipoprotein loss but never names MTTP.
statements.in_paper_where: Results, Transcriptomic Analysis (APOA1, APOA2, LDLR; cholesterol homeostasis) and Integrating Transcriptomics and Proteomics, Figure 6A (cholesterol metabolism)

statements.justification: APOB -5.28 (RNA) and -7.09 (protein) in the DBD mutant, SUMO +0.67/-0.33, match the file. The mouse HNF4α-knockout abstract supports the apoB/MTTP link. It largely repeats S1; 'not through HNF1A abundance' ignores that the paper's own qPCR shows truncated HNF4α fails to drive HNF1A.
statements.in_paper_where: Results, Transcriptomic Analysis (apolipoprotein genes, cholesterol homeostasis); Figure 6A

statements.justification: Directions match (CDH1 RNA -0.46/-1.37, protein -2.92/-3.16), but 'markedly down at both levels' overstates the DBD mRNA (-0.46, under 2-fold). HNF4A promoting E-cadherin is established, though the cited renal-cancer paper is a distant system. The paper reports shared adhesion loss without naming CDH1.
statements.in_paper_where: Results, Integrating Transcriptomics and Proteomics (cell adhesion molecules, focal adhesion in both mutants); Figure 6A

statements.justification: Values match: ITGB5 protein -1.87/-2.02, RNA -0.53/-0.57 (not relevant); PRKCE RNA -2.28 vs -0.12. 'Post-transcriptional' is an inference from a microarray cut-off. The PKCε-integrin evidence is from glioma cells, and ITGB5 loss is shared by both mutants, so a DBD-specific adhesion defect is weakly supported.
statements.in_paper_where: Results, Transcriptomic Analysis and Integrating Transcriptomics and Proteomics (ECM organization, focal adhesion, ECM-receptor interaction)

statements.justification: Values match: DAB2 protein -3.61 vs -0.39, RNA not relevant (-0.45/+0.94), so a post-transcriptional drop is a reasonable reading. Dab2 as an LDLR-family clathrin adaptor is accurate. The closing 'link' between integrin/ECM loss and LDLR endocytosis is loose speculation, not shown by these data.

All values match (PRKCSH RNA -1.48; proteins about -0.9 to -1.0 in the DBD mutant; GANAB and CALR protein-only) and the calnexin-cycle description is correct. Offering this as a possible contributor to the secretory collapse is speculative: APOB mRNA already collapses (-5.28), and reduced secretory load may be the cause of lower chaperones.

Textbook MTTP biology (both citations accurate) that adds nothing about this experiment. The claim that MTTP loss will 'block secretion' of the other apolipoproteins is circular: APOB, APOA1 and APOA4 mRNA are already down, and day-9 progenitors were not shown to secrete VLDL. No lipid or secretion was measured.

Numbers match (HNF1A -0.39/-0.10; four targets down), but the perturbed factor is HNF4A, not HNF1A; nothing shows HNF1A activity is lost, and the paper reports truncated HNF4α fails to drive HNF1A itself. The cited HNF1A POU-mutant liver-cancer paper concerns HNF4A promoter activity, not this allele.

overall.comment: The data readings are accurate throughout, and S1, S2 and S6 correctly capture a large DBD-specific loss of the lipoprotein, secretory and ER-chaperone proteins and a shared adhesion/ECM loss, which matches the paper's cholesterol-metabolism and adhesion enrichments. It never reaches the paper's mitochondrial/respiratory-chain conclusion or the failed hepatoblast specification that probably underlies much of the DBD signature. It frames the experiment around HNF1A (S8, title) when HNF4A was edited, and S7 is generic.
